k-1.summary: Five unnumbered activities (free play, tiny piles, a trap table for 4–9, choosing first or second against the grown-up, and a {1,2,3} extension) build real backward induction with good counter pictures, and every answer is correct (traps 3, 6, 9; then 4, 8, 12). But the pages carry decorative titles, a name line and exclamations; page 2 is nearly trivial; the trap rule is printed as a procedure with a worked row; and the {1,2,3} idea is crammed into a box, so a quick child runs out at about 28 minutes. No activity has a 'Problem N:' label, so the numbered-problem count is 0.

edits.quote: What pattern do the traps make? ... A game starts with 20 counters. Do you want to go first or second? If you go first, how many will you take? Why?
edits.fix: One idea is split into one-line steps. Merge P2–P4 into one problem: mark piles 0–12 W or T, then decide first or second and the first move for 20, with a reason.

edits.quote: Taking 2 is NOT allowed!
edits.fix: Delete; the crossed-out picture and the title already say it.

edits.quote: Careful: if only 2 counters are left, the only move is to take 1!
edits.fix: Delete. It gives away the only trap in P8, and the shared rules already say you cannot take more than the pile has.

edits.quote: Think back to the ends of your games. Was a player ever stuck with a pile they did not want? Which piles were bad to have on your turn? ... Make a guess: with 10 counters, is it better to go first or second?
edits.fix: These are filler follow-ups to P5 that the trap finder answers anyway. Cut to one prompt or delete.

edits.quote: You will check your guess on the next page.
edits.fix: Delete the meta narration.

edits.quote: Play tiny games that start with 1, 2, 3, 4, or 5 counters. ... Pick one trap you found. Explain why every move from it is bad.
edits.fix: Only pile 2 is a trap from 1 to 5, so 'pick one' implies several that do not exist, and the explanation is already printed above. Extend the range to 1–10 (traps 2, 7, 9) and ask why 7 is a trap, or fold P8 into the trap finder.

edits.quote: How to find traps: 0 is a trap. If some move leaves your partner a trap, the pile is a W. If every move leaves your partner a W, the pile is a trap, T. Work from the top down. ... Circle the leftover piles that are traps. Circled one? Write W. None circled? Write T. [table with every leftover pile precomputed, rows 0–2 filled in]
edits.fix: The central classification becomes a lookup: the induction rule is printed and every move is precomputed. It also has no problem number. Number it, give a blank pile / W-or-T table to 20, and keep the rule and the worked rows with the adult.

edits.quote: Check: from 1 to 20 you should find exactly 5 traps. (printed upside down)
edits.fix: Move the answer check to the adult notes.

edits.quote: Check your guess from page 2. Is 10 a W pile or a trap?
edits.fix: Delete; it is a lookup in the row the child just filled. Fold it into P10.

edits.quote: If you start with 10 and go first, how many should you take? [one small box]
edits.fix: Taking 1 (leaves 9) and taking 3 (leaves 7) both win, but the single box implies one answer. Ask: 'Find every first move that wins.'

edits.quote: What makes a strategy work? A winning strategy must have a good answer to every move your partner might make, not just the moves you expect.
edits.fix: This is teaching commentary with a 'not just' construction, and P11–P13 teach the point themselves. Delete; keep 'All the claims use the rule take 1, 3, or 4' inside P11.

edits.quote: Write the traps in order. In each small box, write the jump from one trap to the next. [first jump 0→2 filled] What do you notice about the jumps?
edits.fix: This prints the method for finding the pattern that P14 already asks for. Delete it, or reduce it to 'Describe the pattern so you could decide any pile.'

edits.fix: Replace the label with 'Problem 18:'.

edits.quote: My rule: take ____ [0–15 strip of single W/T boxes]
edits.fix: There is no room to work out moves for a new rule. Give a short pile / moves / W-or-T table or scratch space.

grades-2-3.summary: The math is correct and well chosen: a {1,2} warm-up, a full classification of {1,3,4} to 20 (traps 2, 7, 9, 14, 16), three claims to test against every reply (Ava's 7, Ben's 9, Cleo's greedy rule), the 0-or-2-mod-7 pattern to 39 and beyond (50 is W; 25, take 4), and an invent-a-rule extension. But the central trap finder is turned into a lookup by a printed algorithm and precomputed leftover columns. Several one-line follow-ups break up the investigation, and the titles, box labels, a Name/Partner line and exclamations need trimming.

edits.quote: Working backward. 0 is L (your opponent just took the last counter). A pile is W if at least one move leads to an L pile. A pile is L if every move leads to a W pile.
edits.fix: Keep the W/L definitions and '0 is L'. Let children work out the W/L rule while doing P2, and leave the stated rule with the adult.

edits.quote: Play a few games starting with 10 or 11 counters. Who wins, the first or the second player?
edits.fix: Under {1,2}, 10 and 11 are both first-player wins, so there is no contrast, and in casual play the answer is random. Use 9, 10 and 11, and ask who can make sure to win in each.

edits.quote: Every multiple of 3 is an L pile. Explain why. Your explanation must work against every move your opponent could make. (What do you do after they take 1? After they take 2?)
edits.fix: This states the result P2 asks children to find, and the parenthetical gives the copy-reply strategy. Merge P3 and P4 into 'Which piles are L? Explain why, for every move your opponent could make, and say how to win from the other piles.'

edits.quote: Take 1, 3, or 4 counters (not 2). With 2 counters left, the only move is to take 1.
edits.fix: Delete. '(not 2)' repeats the braces, and the second sentence gives away that 2 is an L pile.

edits.quote: Work from small to large, using the rules for working backward.
edits.fix: Delete the method instruction.

edits.quote: List the L piles you found:
edits.fix: Delete; it copies the grid just filled.

edits.quote: Can you say it using remainders? A pile is L exactly when dividing it by [ ] leaves a remainder of [ ] or [ ].
edits.fix: The template gives away the form of the answer (one divisor, two remainders). Ask: 'Describe which piles are L so that you could decide for any pile.'

edits.quote: 50: [ ] 100: [ ] 1000: [ ] ____ (one short line to explain three predictions; bottom third of the page empty)
edits.fix: Move the empty space at the bottom of the page up under P9 so each prediction has room for a reason.

edits.quote: To label pile n under {1, 3, 4}, you only need the labels of piles n − 1, n − 3, and n − 4. All three sit inside the window of 4 piles just before n. ... Copy your labels from page 2 into these two windows. ... What do you notice? ... [pigeonhole box] ... Hint: think about the windows that start at piles 0, 1, 2, …, 16. ... If the biggest move is 10, how many different windows are possible?
edits.fix: The periodicity proof is printed as copy, notice and count steps. Ask instead which earlier labels are needed to label pile 20, keep the window diagram, then pose one central problem: why must the {1,3,4} pattern repeat forever, and why must every rule whose biggest move is 4 eventually repeat? Move the pigeonhole box and the hint to the adults.

edits.quote: (Hint: every move takes an odd number.)
edits.fix: Delete the hint.

edits.quote: Greedy Gus always takes the biggest number the rule allows. Under {1, 3, 4}, find a pile where Gus’s move loses, but a different move would have won.
edits.fix: After the periodicity work this is one lookup, and the alliterative name is decoration. Ask for every pile up to 29 where taking the most loses but another move wins (5, 8, 10, 12, 15, 17, 19, ...), and ask what pattern those piles make.

edits.quote: Label each position W or L. The cell in row a and column b means ... [7×7 grid]
edits.fix: The two-pile game goes straight to an abstract grid. First have pairs play with two piles of counters, for example 4 and 5, 3 and 3, and 1 and 4.

edits.quote: (Hint: copycat.)
edits.fix: Delete the hint.

edits.quote: Mathematicians give each pile a number called its Grundy value. It tells you more than just W or L.
edits.fix: Delete the narration and start with the mex definition.

edits.quote: Example: from pile 1 you can only move to pile 0 (value 0). The mex of (0) is 1.
edits.fix: Delete; it repeats the pre-filled value for pile 1 ('Two are done for you').

edits.quote: Still unsolved: In some take-away games you may also split a pile into two piles. ... It is a real open question! To read more: Berlekamp, Conway, and Guy, Winning Ways; Siegel, Combinatorial Game Theory.
edits.fix: Move the Guy's-conjecture note and the references to the adult notes.

edits.quote: Six pages and 26 problems introducing induction, the mod-7 pattern, a pigeonhole proof, the two-pile grid and Grundy values in a 40-minute block
edits.fix: Pages 5–6 will not be reached, and each later idea gets thin concrete work. Move the Grundy page to an adult-held extension sheet and spend the space on more play with two piles.

grades-4-5.summary: This is the deepest band, and every answer checks: L piles 0 or 2 mod 7, take 4 from 1000, 16 windows, two-pile L exactly when the piles match mod 3 (so 14 and 20 is L), Grundy values 0,1,0,1,2,3,2 repeating, 4 and 6 an L pair, n = 12. But it scripts the periodicity proof through copy-the-windows, a pigeonhole box and hints, gives away the P2 and P8 discoveries, and packs six pages and five ideas into 40 minutes. The titles, Challenge labels, name field and open-problem box should be cut or moved to the adults.

overall.strongest: Grades 4–5 is the strongest: every claim and answer is correct, and the sequence runs from backward induction through the mod-7 pattern to a pigeonhole proof of periodicity, rule comparisons and Grundy values, needing mostly cuts of hints, headings and the last page.
overall.weakest: K–1 is the weakest: it gives a quick child only about 28 minutes, page 2 is nearly trivial, the trap rule is printed as a procedure with a worked row, the {1,2,3} extension is crammed into a box, and it carries the most cutesy titles and exclamations.
